title: Beyond Relational: Documents, Columns & Partitions
summary: Why analytical engines store data by column and compress it with run-length and dictionary encoding, how document stores query nested data, and how hash and range partitioning spread data out and let queries skip what they don't need.
takeaways: Column stores read only the columns a query touches, and similar values stored together compress very well.
Run-length and dictionary encoding shrink low-cardinality and sorted columns, often by an order of magnitude.
Hash partitioning needs a hash that's stable across processes. Python's built-in hash() of a str isn't.
Range partitioning lets the planner prune partitions. A value equal to a bound belongs to the next partition.

flow.title: A query over a partitioned column store

steps.label: Prune partitions
steps.detail: Compare the WHERE range with each partition's bounds and skip those that can't match.

steps.label: Prune columns
steps.detail: Open only the columns the query references, not whole rows.

steps.label: Decode
steps.detail: Expand dictionary codes and RLE runs back into values, or operate on them directly.

steps.label: Filter + aggregate
steps.detail: Scan the needed columns position by position and accumulate per group.

terms.definition: A layout that stores each column's values contiguously, instead of each row's, as in Parquet, BigQuery or C-Store.
Storing repeated consecutive values as (value, count) pairs.
Replacing each value with a small integer code into a list of distinct values.
Assigning a row to partition hash(key) mod N, so equal keys always land together.
Skipping partitions whose bounds prove they can't contain rows matching the query.
